These findings make anemia, primary pulmonary disease (COPD, obstructive lung disease), and overt systolic heart failure unlikely. In older patients with longstanding hypertension progressive exertional dyspnea with otherwise normal resting tests is most commonly due to impaired left ventricular diastolic function (HFpEF) — symptoms occur with exertion while resting BNP/CXR/oximetry can be normal and ECG nonspecific. Pulmonary embolism or occult malignancy are possible but less likely given subacute month‑long progressive course and lack of supporting features. Definitive diagnosis requires echocardiography with assessment of LVEF and diastolic parameters (and possibly exercise testing), but the clinical picture is most consistent with diastolic heart failure (HFpEF).

[DIAGNOSIS] Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) due to left ventricular diastolic dysfunction.
